articles.title: Akhilesh Yadav visits Azam Khan in jail; vows to bring about BJP’s downfall
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav met party leader Azam Khan in Rampur district Jail on Thursday (October 22, 2026). Mr. Yadav accused the BJP Government of filing false cases against Mr. Khan and added that no family, particularly no political family, has faced as much injustice as Mr. Khan’s kin. Mr. Yadav vowed to defeat the BJP in Uttar Pradesh.

“I came to meet Azam Saheb, and proclaim our respect for him. False cases have been filed against him and his family. . The BJP is responsible for this injustice. But they cannot imprison the truth, even those who plot against him are locked in a prison of their own minds, haunted by the constant fear that tomorrow, when the truth emerges, they will face the consequences of their actions. They agonize constantly thinking about the punishment to come,” said Mr. Yadav, speaking to reporters outside the jail.

The SP chief said, “Corrupt officials and false cases are two key weapons of the BJP government and administration. Whenever the history of BJP injustice is written, Rampur’s name will appear at the top. The conspiracy to close Jauhar University is actually a plot to snatch the right to education from the PDA. Those who closed thousands of schools would certainly not spare a university! These narrow-minded, negative BJP members are against the poor.”

Despite being held in prolonged judicial custody, Mr. Khan, a ten-term former MLA from Rampur, remains a pivotal figure for the party in Rampur and adjoining areas and is considered a leading SP leader from the Muslim community. Recently, the Rampur Development Authority (RDA) issued an order to demolish 38 of the 40 buildings at Mohammad Ali Jauhar University — which is run by Azam Khan — alleging illegal construction. Amid an uproar, the proposed demolition was halted, and the matter is pending in the Divisional Commissioner’s Court.

The SP added that the meeting highlighted the BJP’s campaign against Azam Khan because of his religious identity and political clout. “Samajwadi Party National President Akhilesh Yadav’s visit to Rampur jail is important in many ways, it reiterated the importance of Azam Khan in the Samajwadi Party hierarchy. It is a reply to those leaders who are trying to reduce Azam Khan as a Muslim leader. It also lays bare the BJP’s design to keep Azam Khan in jail on fabricated charges while the demolition order also exposes the Yogi Govt.’s aversion towards Education,” said Sudhir Panwar, a senior Samajwadi Party (SP) leader.

articles.title: Drunk teen behind wheel of SUV rams car, crashes into electricity pole
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A 19-year-old drunk driver behind the wheel of a SUV rammed into a car before crashing into an electricity pole at Peerzadiguda on the Hyderabad–Warangal National Highway on Thursday. The impact caused the couple’s car to flip multiple times, leaving both the occupants injured.

The accident occurred around 6.30 a.m. near Pillar No. 57 of the Uppal–Narapally elevated corridor in Medipally. The injured were identified as Sai Shiva, 30, and his wife Meghana, 28, who were travelling in a Hyundai i10 from LB Nagar towards Narsampet in Warangal district.

According to the Medipally Inspector D. Jalender Reddy, the driver of the SUV, identified as Akun Sabharwal, 19, recorded a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) reading of 238 mg per 100 ml, nearly eight times the permissible limit of 30 mg per 100 ml. He was also found to be driving without a valid licence, while the SUV was being operated with a temporary registration (TR) number and a fake number plate.

The SUV, travelling at high speed, rammed into the i10 from the rear near Peerzadiguda. The SUV subsequently crashed into an electricity pole, which fell onto the vehicle. The injured couple were shifted to a private hospital in Chaitanyapuri for treatment.

The officer said that incident involved as many as 10 violations under the Motor Vehicles Act and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including drunken driving, overspeeding and driving without a valid licence.

“The accident occurred during the early morning hours when the roads were relatively empty owing to the festival holidays. The consequences could have been far more serious, potentially resulting in fatalities, had the collision occurred during peak traffic hours,” said the officer.

The Medipally police registered a case against Sabharwal and the vehicle’s owner, Mangilal, who was accused of allowing a person without a valid driving licence to operate the SUV. Akun was placed under arrest. Further investigation is under way.

Offering a blend of humour, adventure, and traditional storytelling, Return of the Jungle celebrates themes of courage, friendship, and determination. The public, students, educators, and families are warmly encouraged to attend,” the statement added.

articles.title: Face-off with China continues at multiple locations along Arunachal border: ITBP D-G
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Confrontations with Chinese troops continue to take place at multiple sites along the border in Arunachal Pradesh, according to Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) director general Shatrujeet Kapur.
“In the past few-days, a situation arose where face-off happened at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues,” Mr. Kapur said on Thursday.
This is the first official confirmation of the scale of the rising tensions on the north-eastern border since July this year.
Speaking at the Himveer Samman Samaroah, an annual felicitation ceremony for ITBP personnel, Mr. Kapur said ITBP commandos have been active in the continuing confrontations on the Arunachal border.

“Our newly raised Shaurya commandos played an exemplary role in this. ITBP was raised as a mountain guerilla force and we were given border guarding duty along China in 2004,” he said. “We need not leave our original function, and a specialised high altitude mountain fighting force is being set up, distinct than the army. We will soon have one full battalion of Shaurya commandos; high-altitude [deployment] is our strength,” Mr. Kapur added, during the event held at the Central Training College (CTC), Alwar, Rajasthan.

Government sources told The Hindu that since late July, India and China have been engaged in a stand-off at Asaphila near Taksing in Arunachal Pradesh. The Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) have pitched their tents at an elevation, within 6 km to 7 km of India’s perception of the Line of Actual Control (LAC), near the Maja company operating base in Taksing circle of Upper Subansiri district, sources said.

“Sometime in July, during routine patrolling, Indian and Chinese troops came face to face near Maja. After brief confrontation, both sides returned but the Chinese PLA came back in larger number few days later and pitched tents, around 6-7 kms within India’s perception of the LAC,” the source said.

The situation has persisted even though Chinese President Xi Jinping attended the 18th BRICS Summit hosted by India from September 11 to 13, and the two nations have held three high-level border talks since July.

The 36th WMCC (Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs) meeting on India-China border affairs was held on August 6. This was followed by the 25th round of talks between the Special Representatives (SR) on the Boundary Question on August 26 in Beijing, where India was represented by National Security Adviser (NSA) Ajit Doval. On September 6, the first-ever Corps Commander-level meetings between the two armies was held in the Eastern Sector at the Vacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting Point in Arunachal Pradesh. Such meetings have so far largely been held at the Chushul-Moldo Border Meeting Point in eastern Ladakh, particularly after the Galwan Valley clashes in June 2020.

The Army and the ITBP force are deployed along the China border and long range patrols are regularly sent to the forward areas. Due to the weather conditions, such patrols are sent between June and October in Arunachal Pradesh.

The weapons used by the ITBP are 50-years old and modernisation is required, said Mr. Kapur, who is set to retire on October 31. Stressing on the need to invest and develop drone and counter-drone technology, the ITBP chief said that it may not be possible to face China through traditional methods as it has invested a lot in the modernisation of its weapons and infrastructure.

“Drones are something through which a even a small country can challenge a big country We saw how Ukraine has challenged a superpower like Russia. The war was supposed to be over in few days, but 10,000 to 15,000 Russian soldiers are being killed, they are suffering. Look at Iran, how, without even a Navy, they, with the help of drones, challenged America,” he said.

articles.title: Delhi conference to explore new markets for Indian rice
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Trade and business representatives from over 150 countries will attend the Bharat International Rice Conference (BIRC) beginning in Delhi on Friday (October 23, 2026). Organised by the Indian Rice Exporters Federation (IREF), the three-day conference brings together exporters, importers, millers, policymakers and food businesses to explore new markets, assess the 2027 price outlook and identify ways to earn more from rice.

It will see 65 speakers participating in nine knowledge sessions and 2,038 scheduled business meetings to connect India’s rice industry with global markets. “We want exporters to find new customers, buyers to discover suitable products and millers to identify where they can improve returns. The next chapter of India’s rice trade must be about creating more value, not simply selling more tonnes,” said Dev Garg, national vice-president, IREF. The nine sessions will cover crop surveys and price forecasting; new export markets; documentation, insurance and credit; bulk and container shipping; quality and certification; policy and incentives; sustainability; profitable rice milling; and value-added products.

After the recent war on Iran, one of the major buyers of Indian rice, and the crisis in West Asia, the IREF had been urging the Union government to help the exporters find new markets and assistance in clearing cargos stuck in Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Indian missions in Saudi Arabia working to facilitate early return of stranded pilgrims
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Amid escalating attacks by Yemeni Houthi (Ansar Allah) forces on Saudi Arabia, Indian missions in Riyadh and Jeddah are working with stakeholders to facilitate the early return of thousands of stranded Indian pilgrims, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Thursday (October 22, 2026).

“Our embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate in Jeddah are actively engaging with concerned airlines and tour operators to facilitate the early return of affected pilgrims. Over the past week, about 3,000 stranded Umrah pilgrims have travelled from Saudi Arabia back to India on available flights,” said MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal.

He said volunteers from the Indian community in Saudi Arabia are also assisting the ongoing official efforts. International flight connections to Saudi Arabia have been disrupted following Houthi attacks on several major airports in the country, including the capital, Riyadh, and Dammam. Besides Indians, many pilgrims from other countries are also stranded in Saudi Arabia.
“Arrangements are being discussed to facilitate the return of other Umrah pilgrims at the earliest,” said Mr. Jaiswal.

Meanwhile, the MEA strongly condemned the continued attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including the attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oil field in the Eastern Province on October 21.

“We also reiterate that the attacks on civilian and critical infrastructure are completely unacceptable and must cease immediately. We stand in solidarity with the people and the Government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its sovereignty, and hope that peace and normalcy would return to the region at the earliest,” said the MEA statement.

Earlier, AIMIM chief and Lok Sabha MP Asaduddin Owaisi took to social media to flag the plight of around 4,000 Indian pilgrims who had flown to Saudi Arabia for pilgrimage but were stranded because Indian carriers like IndiGo, Air India and Akasa Air had cancelled their flights due to the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabian airports.

Mr. Owaisi called for “urgent intervention” from the Government of India and said, “The DGCA must give these airlines permission to run flights with large aircraft so that these stranded pilgrims can return to India. If not, at least specified flights must be arranged to bring them back.”

Earlier on Thursday, the spokesperson of the Houthi forces said that a large boat carrying 14 Indians came under attack near the Red Sea close to the Bab al-Mandeb, the vital strait that connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.

Indian officials have not confirmed any assistance reaching the struck boat so far while the Indian embassy in Yemen has said, “We have seen reports regarding an incident involving 14 Indian nationals on board a yacht off the coast of Yemen today. We are ascertaining further details about the incident and will provide all possible help for ensuring the safety and well-being of the Indian nationals.”

articles.title: SBI’s cyber defences under scrutiny; its Cyber Defence Centre to be operational by FY27
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The suspected customer-data exposure at State Bank of India (SBI) has brought its cybersecurity preparedness into focus, despite the bank reporting an extensive array of safeguards in its annual disclosures.

SBI’s FY2025–26 Sustainability Report and Annual Report, published before the reported exposure, detail its security audits, automated threat monitoring, incident-response procedures and employee training. The disclosures also outline plans to further integrate its cyber-defence operations.

SBI’s Sustainability Report says information-systems audits covered 427 IT systems during FY26. Audits of outsourced IT activities covered 695 activities, while internal and external cybersecurity audits covered 176 IT applications and infrastructure and 151 systems, respectively.
However, the report does not disclose the findings, the number of vulnerabilities identified or how many were rectified. SBI reported “nil” instances of data breaches during FY26.

The bank’s Global Cyber Security Operations Centre (GCSOC) continuously monitors critical information systems for threats and unauthorised access. Automated tracking of indicators of compromise (IoCs)—digital clues that may signal cyberattacks—has replaced a previously manual process.
SBI also monitors phishing, fraudulent websites, brand impersonation, vishing and rogue mobile applications, pursuing the removal of malicious links and websites.

Its Annual Report cites an automated Secure Configuration Monitoring System covering more than 85,000 IT assets. AI-driven intelligence platforms, risk profiling and continuous monitoring of digital transactions help identify suspicious activity.

Security testing includes ethical hacking, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing and red-team exercises across websites, mobile applications, databases, networks and internal systems. Monthly domain-password-spray tests seek to identify employees using easily guessed passwords.
Firewalls, encryption, multi-factor authentication and data-loss prevention tools provide additional safeguards.

articles.title: The broken promise of the right to work
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: On August 21, a three-judge Supreme Court Bench led by the Chief Justice of India dismissed a petition and sought a fresh one in a case on minimum wages in rural employment guarantee programmes. The Bench lauded MGNREGA’s role in rural development. It probed whether the ‘Right to Work’ should be treated on par with Article 21, the fundamental right to life, sparking an important discussion on the constitutional foundations of this right.

Despite its limited scope of only 100 days of work per rural household and chronic underfunding, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) was the only law anchored in the core principle of the right to work. In December 2025, the Union government replaced MGNREGA with the Viksit Bharat — Guarantee for Rozgar & Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-GRAM G) Act, and its implementation began on July 1. About 3.44 crore households worked for about 44 crore person-days under MGNREGA in July and August, on average, over the previous five years (Table 1) . There has been a 68% decrease in employment in July and August this year compared with the average of the preceding five years. Notwithstanding the proverbial ‘teething issues’, the dismantling of MGNREGA’s demand-driven right-to-work framework and the disproportionate fiscal burden that the new law places on States are likely to be major factors behind the dramatic fall in employment under the VB-GRAM G Act.

The impact of taking away even this limited right to work is therefore palpable. Discussions around the recent Supreme Court observations on the right to work can be traced back to the Constituent Assembly debates.

While most members agreed that a right to work was vital, the debate rested on whether it should be a fundamental right or be part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP). The DPSPs do not automatically constitute rights but are meant to serve as precepts for governments to formulate laws and policies. This became the basis of the differences in perspective.

Professor K.T. Shah had strongly advocated recognising the right to work as a fundamental right, arguing that the State needed a constitutional and positive legal mandate to guarantee socio-economic security to its citizens. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, among others, held that while the right to work was an essential goal, its immediate universal enforcement was not fiscally and institutionally viable in a newly independent India that had been hollowed out of its resources. The placement of the right within the Directive Principles, rather than among the fundamental rights, thus reflected a deliberate constitutionalism of aspiration, rather than an abandonment of the welfare ideal. As scholars Anjani Kapoor and Manu Bhagwan have written in their essay ‘Ambedkar and the anti-isolation of Fellowship’, “The constitution does not establish the nation, but rather provides the tools to help achieve it.”

Therefore, Article 41 of the DPSP states: ‘The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work…” Embodying stronger progressive consecrations, Articles 39, 42 and 43 call for the “right to an adequate means of livelihood, equal pay for equal work for both men and women, just and humane conditions of work” and to “secure to all workers a living wage and decent standard of life.”

The Supreme Court, in Olga Tellis vs Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), ruled that the right to livelihood was a necessary condition for the fundamental right to life, giving a judicial fillip to the right to work. Spurred by the collective efforts of activists and rural workers, the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was passed in 2005. Although limited in scope, it made a pan-India right-to-work law a reality for the first time. The State had to ensure its statutory obligation to provide employment at minimum wages.

In 2009, MGNREGA wages were delinked from the Minimum Wages Act, 1948. Over time, MGNREGA wages barely kept pace with inflation and continued to remain lower than the minimum agricultural wages in most States. Low wages and an inadequate budget for generating employment have resulted in a steep decline in household earnings, with estimated total household earnings halving in July and August this year compared with the same months last year (Figure 1) .

During the recent hearing, the Supreme Court Bench remarked that if financial resources remained the same, having a minimum wage threshold could reduce the number of workers who could be provided employment. This remark, which appears to align with the Union government’s approach to employment guarantee, merits scrutiny on at least two counts.

First, it vitiates the judgment in Sanjit Roy vs State of Rajasthan (1983) where the Supreme Court observed that payment of wages below minimum wages violates Article 23 of the Constitution and is akin to ‘forced labour.’ Second, it rests on a misleading economic logic that financial resources to implement a welfare programme must remain unchanged and constrained.

In reality, higher wages for rural workers increase their purchasing power, enhance their freedoms, and improve human development outcomes. These, in turn, increase effective demand for goods and services, creating a positive multiplier effect, resulting in higher economic productivity. Therefore, higher government spending on an employment guarantee programme at increased wages can yield a mutually reinforcing cycle between development and growth.

By putting an arbitrary cap on funds for the VB-GRAM G Act and not linking it with minimum wages, the very notion of employment guarantee stands delegitimised. States are already grappling with fiscal constraints and curtailed borrowing limits under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) framework. The increased burden of funding the VB-GRAM G Act will prevent States from generating employment. The sharp drop in employment and earnings is a reflection of this change.

articles.title: Agrivoltaics on 10% of suitable land can meet 2050 power demand: Pralhad Joshi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Operationalising just 10% of the agricultural land deemed suitable for agrivoltaics in India could generate enough electricity to meet the country’s projected power demand for 2050, Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi said on Tuesday.

“If even 10% [of the land deemed suitable for agrivoltaics] is converted [towards operationalisation], more than whatever power requirement is being estimated for 2050 can be generated by agrivoltaics,” he said, citing a study by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI).
Published in July, the study identified about 47.5 million hectares, or nearly 30% of India’s more than 160 million hectares of arable agricultural land, as suitable for agrivoltaics.

The approach combines agricultural activity with solar photovoltaic power generation on the same land, potentially allowing farmers to retain agricultural production while earning additional income from renewable energy.

The government is working on a dedicated policy framework for the sector, with agrivoltaics potentially being incorporated into the next phase of the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (PM-KUSUM).
“We will be launching one of the world’s agrivoltaic programmes under the next phase of PM Kusum,” Mr. Joshi said at the inauguration of the seventh Agrivoltaics World Conference.

Speaking at the conference, Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan highlighted the potential benefits of agrivoltaics but stressed the need to address land-use concerns and assess the feasibility of projects across different regions.

Mr. Joshi said agrivoltaic installations, which typically require elevated solar panel structures to facilitate farming underneath, could cost 25-30% more than conventional ground-mounted solar projects.
He stressed the need to bridge the cost differential to make the model commercially viable.

“The average cost of electricity supply was around ₹7 per unit in [fiscal year] 2025-26. While some of the major agrivoltaics assessment indicate potential generation of ₹3.20 to 3.30 [per unit], whereas ground mounted costs now ₹2.5 to 2.6 [per unit]. This difference has to be matched,” he said.

Mr. Chouhan said the proposed policy must provide mechanisms to help farmers repair solar modules, address disputes and clarify the terms under which agricultural land can be sold or leased, even as he hailed agrivoltaics’ potential for additional revenue generation.
“There must be participation [from farmers] but coinciding with mechanisms to facilitate resolutions as well,” he said.

articles.title: Rupee strengthens for eighth consecutive day on IPO inflows; rise in crude prices cap gains
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The rupee strengthened for the eighth consecutive session on Wednesday (October 21, 2026), buoyed by foreign fund inflows linked to the Jio Platforms IPO. However, a sharp rise in crude oil prices capped its gains amid concerns over imported inflation.

The rupee closed at 94.46 against the U.S. dollar, its strongest level in over a month, after touching an intraday high of 94.43. It pared some gains as benchmark Brent crude prices climbed to $110 a barrel.

The $3.2-billion Jio Platforms IPO, India’s largest initial public offering, opened for subscription on Wednesday (October 21) and was fully subscribed as foreign investors rushed to participate in the issue.

“Going forward, movements in the dollar index, crude oil prices and foreign portfolio flows will remain key drivers, with geopolitical uncertainty continuing to pose risks to the currency,” Anil Kumar Bhansali, head of treasury at Finrex Treasury Advisors LLP, said in a note.

In contrast to the rupee’s gains, the benchmark 10-year government securities (G-Sec) yield rose to 7.44% on Wednesday (October 21, 2026), its highest level since 2023, as surging crude prices intensified inflationary concerns. Bond prices and yields move inversely.

Uncertainty over a resolution to the ongoing West Asia crisis, coupled with concerns over imported inflation, continued to weigh on the bond market. India’s retail inflation rose to a higher-than-expected 5.54% in September, bringing it closer to the Reserve Bank of India’s upper tolerance limit of 6%.
Venkatkrishnan Srinivasan, founder and managing partner of Rockfort Fincap LLP, expects the benchmark 10-year yield to trade in the 7.25%-7.50% range.
“On a durable basis, if the crude remains above $100 for the next 25 days, yields could even rise as high as 7.60%,” he said.

articles.title: Anticipation over upcoming EU FTA more than doubles Ferrari orders in India
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Ferrari has seen more than a doubling of its orders from India in anticipation of the Free Trade Agreement (FTA) between India and the European Union that is set to come into force in early 2027, top officials of the luxury car company said. The FTA will see a substantial lowering of import tariffs on European cars entering the Indian market.

Speaking at a select media roundtable in New Delhi, Ferrari’s heads for Southeast Asia, and the Far and Middle East further said that, over the last two years, the company has restructured itself internally to forefront India in its global plans.

So many of the people are already walking to our dealership every day to say, ‘okay, I know the FTA is coming, can I start to configure my car, can I start to have an idea of the price, etc’,” Charles Antoine Geneste, Head of Southeast Asia at Ferrari said. “So, we can clearly see the passion that was there, and that there is this acceleration that for us is amazing to see.”

Since Ferrari typically likes to maintain a waiting period of 18 months between placing an order and delivery of a car, Mr. Geneste said that customers in India are already lining up to place orders so that they can get delivery once the FTA is in effect.

While declining to quantify exactly how much demand has increased in anticipation of the FTA, when asked if it has doubled, Ferrari’s President of Far and Middle East Francesco Bianchi said: “See, this is big, it’s more than what you say.”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to be in Brussels on December 16 for the signing of the India-EU FTA, and the European authorities say that it is expected to come into force in “early 2027” once the European Parliament has cleared it.

Under the deal, India has agreed to slash import duties on European-made luxury car Completely Built Units (CBUs) from around 110% to 30-35% in the first year, which will further drop to 10% in a phased manner, subject to initial annual quotas.

Ferrari has currently opened its experiential exhibition ‘Universo Ferrari’ in New Delhi up to November 1, where it showcases its key models, including the Formula One race car as well as its Le Mans model, apart from its various luxury streetcars.

This exhibition, so far launched in only five countries worldwide, including its home country of Italy, is the latest in a series of moves Ferrari has made over the last few years to increasingly cater to the India market.

“We deliberately decided to have a team that is focused on India and Southeast Asia,” Mr Bianchi said. “We found that the previous structure that we had was not effective enough to really expand the potential of a market like India.”

“We prefer to grant India maximum visibility,” he added. “So, basically the team that is also managing the Southeast Asia markets is now owning India and India is for sure the main engine of this region.”

articles.title: UN climate damages fund earmarks $20 million to Nepal for August disaster
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The United Nations climate convention’s Loss and Damage Fund has set aside $21.6 million for Nepal towards addressing the damage from the Bhotekoshi floods that ravaged the country in August.

The decision, taken at an extraordinary meeting by the Fund’s Board on Thursday (October 22, 2026), is the first time that the Fund has earmarked money for a specific country to remedy damage from climate change. However, the funds still constitute a tiny fraction of the $5 billion in economic losses the country has self assessed.
It comes weeks before the 31st UN climate conference, COP31, opens in Turkey next month.

On August 26, a climate-induced ice-and-rock avalanche in Nepal set off a debris flow and flooding along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli-Narayani river system. The Nepal government puts initial recovery and reconstruction needs at a minimum of $4.71 billion.

On August 31, Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, and Agriculture, Forests and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary wrote to the Board’s co-chairs. They asked it to “take a special decision to respond rapidly, directly and effectively.” The letter said that Nepal, a least developed country, contributes negligibly to global emissions yet bears escalating climate impacts, and that the full extent of losses was still to be determined.

Board members from Africa, Asia-Pacific and least developed countries then sought an extraordinary meeting. Members from Latin America, small island states, Eastern Europe and developed countries sent letters of support.

The Fund for responding to Loss and Damage, was established at COP27 in 2022, with its operational mechanism agreed at COP28 the following year. It is meant to help vulnerable developing countries respond to economic and non-economic losses from climate change.

The Fund has pledges by countries (mostly developed) of more than $820 million, of which $342 million has been promised for its start-up phase. On the other hand, it has 176 requests from 119 countries, worth about $2.8 billion. There was no official figure immediately available on how much money the Fund had on hand, and the disbursement, even in the Nepal case, will rest on donors making good on their pledges in time.

The allocation, as of Thursday, is provisional and includes $1.6 million in “oversight fees,” which are a charge the Fund pays to the organisations that implement its projects, to cover the cost of overseeing how the money is used. These can include multilateral banks, national institutions, and UN agencies.

“The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) has taken a landmark operational step by allocating $20 million for the reconstruction in Nepal following the [glacial lake outburst flood] GLOF event. But the funding is less than 0.5% of Nepal’s estimated $5 billion reconstruction costs, and the cash would be released only after Nepal clears further bureaucratic project proposals, risking a delay to vital relief amid an ongoing structural crisis. I would suggest that the FLRD releases support immediately if the bulk of funding is coming from other sources,” Ajay Mathur, former Director General, International Solar Alliance, said in a statement.

fullParagraphs: A retired U.S. teacher freed by President Vladimir Putin after four years' detention in Russia for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine has returned to the United States, his lawyer said on Thursday (October 22, 2026).
"Yes he has landed back," Stephen Hubbard's lawyer Martin De Luca told AFP , without providing details.
U.S. President Donald Trump posted photos early Thursday (October 22, 2026) showing Mr. Hubbard smiling as he posed with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff.
Another photo showed the former English teacher, who is in his 70s, posing with unidentified people on a small plane, holding up an American flag with two members of the group.

Mr. Trump said Mr. Hubbard was released without the United States having to agree to a prisoner swap. However the Republican leader lifted some sanctions on Russia ahead of the release and also agreed to purchase Russian diesel — a boon to the Kremlin's ability to finance its continued invasion of Ukraine.

Mr. Witkoff was in Russia on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) to meet with Mr. Putin. The Russian leader said afterward that Moscow was ready in principle to rejoin talks with Ukraine and the United States to end the war.

Mr. Hubbard's family and lawyers have said he was living in the Ukrainian city of Izium when he was taken captive by Russia in 2022. He was sentenced to almost seven years in prison, accused of acting as a "mercenary" for Kyiv. He denies the charges.
A Ukrainian who was held with Mr. Hubbard told AFP that the American was tortured in custody.

articles.title: Albanian lawmakers scuffle in parliament as protests continue

fullParagraphs: Albanian lawmakers grappled on the floor of parliament on Thursday (October 22, 2026), as the opposition accused the government of violently targeting protesters over a week of unrest in the capital.
Since last week, student demonstrators have taken to the streets to demand better support for education and to renew months-long calls for Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation.
Protesters have routinely clashed with police and attacked government buildings, with more than 300 people, including many officers, injured and dozens of protesters detained.
On Thursday (October 22, 2026), during a scheduled vote, opposition MPs gathered in front of the speaker's podium, calling for the session to be stopped because of the unrest.

The group held pictures showing the face and wounds of a protester allegedly injured by officers. Water and documents were lobbed towards the speaker, triggering a scuffle with other parliamentarians.
Dramatic scenes in the Albanian parliament are not unusual, with similar scenes erupting in the past and flares lit in the chamber at least twice.

"Opposition MPs decided today to serve as the voice for the demands of the student protests," Sali Berisha, longtime opposition leader and head of the Democratic Party, said in a statement.v"This parliament cannot continue; it lacks legitimacy."
Socialist Party MP Pirro Vengu, from Rama's ruling party, in a post on social media accused the opposition of trying to "use the unrest as a path to return to power".
Several hundred protesters gathered outside parliament on Thursday (October 22, 2026) during the session, but no clashes were reported.
The protesters have clearly distanced themselves from any political party, and regularly carry signs accusing both Rama and Berisha of corruption.

On Wednesday evening (October 21, 2026), only minor sporadic incidents occurred on the streets of Tirana. But the student-led protest movement has called for a national rally on Saturday (October 24, 2026).
Anti-government protests in the Balkan nation began in May over a controversial resort development linked to US President Donald Trump's family.

articles.title: Myanmar's Suu Kyi sounded 'fairly healthy', son says after first call in years
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The son of Myanmar's Aung San Suu Kyi said she sounded "fairly healthy" after speaking to the detained ex-democratic leader on Thursday for the first time in more than five years.
Suu Kyi, 81, is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
"She was sounding fairly healthy," her son, Kim Aris said after the telephone conversation, which he said was the first time he had spoken to his mother in more than five years.

Aung San Suu Kyi's son, Kim Aris, talks on the phone with his mother, Myanmar's former leader, who is in Naypyitaw, Myanmar, from Myanmar's embassy in London, Britain, on October 22, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters
"She was able to say she was in good health, but being 81, things aren't getting any better," said Aris, who lives in the United Kingdom.

News of the conversation was the second rare update on Ms. Suu Kyi this week, after Myanmar authorities on Monday (October 19, 2026)published pictures of her receiving a package sent by Britain's King Charles III.
Analysts say Myanmar's rulers are increasingly advertising Ms. Suu Kyi's wellbeing and her contacts with the outside world, as they bid to shake off their post-coup pariah status abroad.
"Essentially we just discussed family matters," Mr. Aris said, adding: "We knew the phone call would be recorded, so we didn't talk about anything sensitive."

Myanmar's presidential spokesperson released photographs of Ms. Suu Kyi and Mr. Aris speaking into telephones, the detained Nobel Peace Prize laureate sitting under a calendar marked with Thursday's date.
A statement said the pair had a "consular telephone conversation" for 20 minutes starting at 2:30 pm (0800 GMT), and that Aris had taken the call from Myanmar's embassy in London.
"She was most concerned about my health and the rest of the family: that was her first question, if I was well," Mr. Aris told AFP . "I remain very concerned about her wellbeing."

articles.title: UN climate damages fund earmarks $20 million to Nepal for August disaster
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The United Nations climate convention’s Loss and Damage Fund has set aside $21.6 million for Nepal towards addressing the damage from the Bhotekoshi floods that ravaged the country in August.

The decision, taken at an extraordinary meeting by the Fund’s Board on Thursday (October 22, 2026), is the first time that the Fund has earmarked money for a specific country to remedy damage from climate change. However, the funds still constitute a tiny fraction of the $5 billion in economic losses the country has self assessed.
It comes weeks before the 31st UN climate conference, COP31, opens in Turkey next month.

On August 26, a climate-induced ice-and-rock avalanche in Nepal set off a debris flow and flooding along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli-Narayani river system. The Nepal government puts initial recovery and reconstruction needs at a minimum of $4.71 billion.

On August 31, Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, and Agriculture, Forests and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary wrote to the Board’s co-chairs. They asked it to “take a special decision to respond rapidly, directly and effectively.” The letter said that Nepal, a least developed country, contributes negligibly to global emissions yet bears escalating climate impacts, and that the full extent of losses was still to be determined.

Board members from Africa, Asia-Pacific and least developed countries then sought an extraordinary meeting. Members from Latin America, small island states, Eastern Europe and developed countries sent letters of support.

The Fund for responding to Loss and Damage, was established at COP27 in 2022, with its operational mechanism agreed at COP28 the following year. It is meant to help vulnerable developing countries respond to economic and non-economic losses from climate change.

The Fund has pledges by countries (mostly developed) of more than $820 million, of which $342 million has been promised for its start-up phase. On the other hand, it has 176 requests from 119 countries, worth about $2.8 billion. There was no official figure immediately available on how much money the Fund had on hand, and the disbursement, even in the Nepal case, will rest on donors making good on their pledges in time.

The allocation, as of Thursday, is provisional and includes $1.6 million in “oversight fees,” which are a charge the Fund pays to the organisations that implement its projects, to cover the cost of overseeing how the money is used. These can include multilateral banks, national institutions, and UN agencies.

“The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) has taken a landmark operational step by allocating $20 million for the reconstruction in Nepal following the [glacial lake outburst flood] GLOF event. But the funding is less than 0.5% of Nepal’s estimated $5 billion reconstruction costs, and the cash would be released only after Nepal clears further bureaucratic project proposals, risking a delay to vital relief amid an ongoing structural crisis. I would suggest that the FLRD releases support immediately if the bulk of funding is coming from other sources,” Ajay Mathur, former Director General, International Solar Alliance, said in a statement.

articles.title: E-rickshaw battery ‘hacks’ and Bluetooth BMS vulnerabilities | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The story so far: Over the last week, social media has been flooded with videos depicting individuals using mobile applications such as BAT-BMS, Lossigy and Epoch-i-ion to wirelessly disable the batteries of e-rickshaws using Bluetooth. The videos have largely been shared as “pranks” — however cruel, unethical and unlawful they may be — while some have speculated that the applications were designed for high-tech sabotage by China’s manufacturers. The reality is far less dramatic, yet still worth understanding carefully.

Applications such as BAT-BMS exist to allow fleet owners and service technicians to easily diagnose battery problems such as overvoltage or undervoltage. In most vehicles, battery management and diagnostics require physical access to the module and the use of a computer or other device to gather information.

Over time, manufacturers have begun equipping these modules with Bluetooth capabilities, making diagnostics and repairs easier without requiring extensive disassembly. Applications such as BAT-BMS are typically developed alongside the battery management systems they support and are almost certainly not intended to sow chaos by disabling as many vehicles as possible. Instead, they search for specific devices advertising themselves as battery management modules over Bluetooth, connect to one device at a time, display diagnostic information, and provide basic debugging functions.

The BAT-BMS application is specifically designed to discover and connect to BMS modules manufactured by a Chinese electronics company, Jiabaida. A seven-year-old public discussion on the open source code sharing platform GitHub documented a lack of authentication in Jiabaida BMS modules, with the author even providing a hacky workaround for this obvious security flaw.

Over time, this vulnerability appears to have been discovered and subsequently exploited by individuals who began popularising its misuse. In particular, some users circulated short-form “prank” videos demonstrating how it could be used to disable e-rickshaw batteries.

Almost all of the components that make up e-rickshaws are imported from China. In fact, one could order almost all the parts required to assemble one from consumer websites such as Alibaba Group or AliExpress. Of course, one could go even further and import a fully pre-assembled e-rickshaw from China through these platforms, though the shipping fees and Customs duties might eat into your margin. Most manufacturers import the electronic components required to assemble e-rickshaws from China, leaving only the fabrication and assembly of the aluminium frame and chassis to be done domestically.

It appears that whenever something goes wrong, the government is quick enough to attribute blame to digital platforms. Telegram was ordered to be blocked during the Re-NEET period, reportedly to protect individuals from fraudsters claiming to sell leaked examination question papers in advance. Similarly, following viral “prank” incidents, the government directed Google and Apple to remove several popular battery management apps from their respective app stores.

In both cases, the government has chosen to restrict access to applications rather than address the underlying issues in a meaningful way. While the two applications are fundamentally different — one being a widely used communication platform with social media features, and the other a set of utilities for diagnosing battery issues — the reasoning behind both decisions appears similar. In essence, when a particular technology becomes associated with harm, restricting access to that technology is seen as a way to eliminate the harm itself.

Hypothetically, if the Re-NEET examination were to be compromised, the breach would have to occur at the source or during transit — during question formulation, printing, or transport. The breach would not originate from, nor be enabled by, the Telegram platform itself. Blocking Telegram in this hypothetical scenario would only temporarily disrupt the sale of leaked question papers, until sellers migrate to another platform of choice. Similarly, restricting battery management applications does not make vulnerable BMS modules any more secure. If anything, it might further inconvenience users who have been affected and are trying to restore functionality to their vehicles.

Contrary to popular belief, regulatory frameworks governing e-rickshaws do exist. Gazette notifications GSR 709(E) dated 8.10.2014 and S.O. 2590(E) dated 8.10.2014 define requirements related to overall dimensions, tyres, brakes, horns, and vehicle identification number standards, but do not provide detailed standards for electronic components.

Globally, as security risks become increasingly associated with the supply chains, various strategies have been adopted to address vulnerabilities before a product reaches the assembly line. These include vetting suppliers, auditing the firmware of electronic components, and tracing the origin and capabilities of individual parts. Such measures can be mandated through regulation. A simple Google search conducted seven years ago could have alerted e-rickshaw manufacturers to the security issues in the BMS modules they use.

Frameworks that establish standards, as well as responsibilities and liabilities for manufacturers, should ideally extend to all products containing electronic components, not just vehicles or specifically e-rickshaws. While sourcing parts from the cheapest available source might be suitable for building a quick prototype, the long-term production and marketing of products should require greater effort and due diligence than simply placing a few orders and setting up an assembly line.

articles.title: Greens see red over Keralam government move to permit sand extraction in 17 rivers
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Environmental activists have expressed concerns about the impact of the Keralam government’s reported decision to permit extraction of 1.7 crore tonnes of sand from 17 rivers across the State from December 2026.

Functionaries of the Society for the Protection of the Environment, Kerala (SPEK) say that although this is presented as a flood mitigation step, no environmental impact assessment seems to have been conducted. SPEK president K. Koyatty and secretary K.K. Devadasan point out that it could also serve as a pretext for indiscriminate extraction of sand from all rivers and streams. The claim that dredging silt from a river prevents flooding lacks clarity, they say.

Mr. Koyatty says every river is a complex system, spanning various stages from its source to where it meets the ocean. It consists not only of water, but also of sand, soil, organic matter, aquatic plants, and aquatic life. “A river cannot truly be a river without sand. The presence of sand in a river is essential for controlling floods, facilitating the seepage of water into the soil which is later preserved as groundwater, and ensuring the retention of water in paddy fields, wetlands, wells and other waterbodies. Agriculture, irrigation, fisheries, and various development works are all founded upon this ecosystem, which has evolved over long periods,” he says.

The environmental activists highlight the role of rivers in replenishing wells, one of the main sources of drinking water in rural areas, which also help maintain the groundwater level. “When sand is extracted from rivers, which is also called channel mining, the riverbed is lowered. Consequently, sunlight is unable to reach the bottom of the river. As a result, the vegetation and other plant life on the riverbed do not receive the necessary sunlight, preventing photosynthesis and leading to their destruction. Small fish that depend on these organisms, as well as the larger fish that feed on them, perish. The ecosystem along the riverbank is shattered. The survival of benthic organisms, or bottom-dwelling aquatic life, is affected too. This impacts the livelihoods of the fishing community,” Mr. Devadasan says.

The activists also say that flooding is mainly caused by the reclamation of the flood plains of rivers and construction activities, and not through accumulation of sand. Another reason for flooding is the sudden, intense rainfall or the massive surge of water resulting from the abrupt opening of dams, they say. In urban areas, flooding is primarily caused by the blockage of drains that lead into rivers, as well as the reclamation of wetlands, the SPEK functionaries claim.

However, the activists also admit that since sand is essential for the construction sector, it may be removed in limited quantities, based on precise studies and in proportion to the amount that accumulates over time in check dams and rivers. They demand that a precise legal framework must be established to regulate sand extraction from rivers, specifying the permissible quantity, the timing and method of extraction, and the exact locations.

Mr. Koyatty and Mr. Devadasan say sand extraction may only be carried out in strict adherence to the directives and supervision of a monitoring committee, which shall comprise representatives from relevant government departments, such as Revenue, Environment, and Local Self-Governments. Large-scale, widespread mechanical and manual sand extraction will only devastate the 44 rivers and their ecosystems in the State, they add.
SPEK is organising a discussion on the issue in Kozhikode on October 24 to commemorate environmental activist A. Achyuthan.

articles.title: What is PHP and why is it facing a security crisis | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Story so far: On October 21, 2026, the team behind PHP announced two serious security flaws. In simple terms, a hacker could use them to break into a website’s server from far away, without needing physical access or a password. Security experts around the world have warned that the flaws could let attackers take control of affected servers.
PHP is a programming language that runs behind the scenes on websites. You never see it, but you use it all the time.

Say you log into your bank’s website or book a movie ticket. Your details travel to a server, which checks who you are, looks up your information and sends back the right page. PHP is often the tool doing that work.

It’s especially common in the systems that power online shops, blogs, news sites, membership sites and business tools. If something goes wrong with PHP, a lot of websites can be affected at once. That’s true whether it’s a small shop on cheap shared hosting or a big company with hundreds of servers.

Think of a computer’s memory as a huge set of shelves. Programs put things on the shelves, take them off and tidy up when they’re done. Good software has to keep careful track of what’s where, especially when something goes wrong halfway through a task.
The two flaws are both mistakes in this tidying-up process.

The first is a problem with running out of space. When PHP runs low on memory, it can end up handling half-finished data badly while cleaning up. This can leave the shelves in a mess, which is called “memory corruption.”

The second is a stale note. In some error situations, PHP keeps a note pointing to a shelf that has already been cleared. Later, it tries to use what it thinks is there, but finds something else entirely.

A skilled attacker can sometimes use these messes to sneak in their own instructions and make the server run them. That’s called “remote code execution.” If PHP has enough permissions on the server, an attacker could read private data, steal passwords or change what your website shows.

There’s another catch. These flaws sit deep inside PHP itself, so they can be triggered before a website’s own protections, such as login checks, get a chance to step in. A website can have strong security of its own and still be exposed.

According to the PHP Foundation, the group that supports PHP, the first flaw was spotted in 2024 during a security review. It took a long time to sort out, and the Foundation has admitted there were delays. Both flaws were made public this month, along with fixes.

That doesn’t mean hackers have been using them for two years. Finding a flaw, working out whether it can really be abused, reporting it safely and proving someone actually attacked are all separate steps.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

articles.title: Fall of the centre: on the public discontent in France
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: When Emmanuel Macron came to power in 2017 , at age 39, he promised to keep extremist political forces at bay, build a new France through his ‘revolution’, rejuvenate economic growth, manage debt and create employment opportunities. Nine years later, with six months to go for France’s next presidential election, Mr. Macron, whose approval rating is at an abysmally low 15%, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu , who lacks a parliamentary majority, are struggling to restore order in a country battered by economic woes, street protests, violent riots and a surging far right. Even in France, where protests are part of the political culture, Saturday’s (October 17, 2026) riots and looting were a shock with at least 3,000 businesses and shops damaged. Municipal halls were attacked and buildings set on fire , including the 19 th -century Limoges town hall. Some 2,400 people were arrested and Prime Minister Lecornu called for local curfews . The trigger for the unrest was a move by Mr. Lecornu to pass budget proposals raising some taxes and freezing spending on social programmes. When school students hit the streets with demands for better educational facilities, the government responded with force and tear gas. But its heavy-handed response helped the student protest snowball into an anti-government movement, culminating in riots.

To understand the precarious situation France is in today, all one has to do is to look at the macroeconomic numbers. Growth remains sluggish with the economy estimated to expand by a mere 0.8% in 2026, while the unemployment rate stands at 8.3%. The core problem is the country’s public finances. France’s national debt stands at 120% of GDP, the third highest in the eurozone, after Greece and Italy. The French Treasury’s debt servicing bill is expected to reach about €60 billion in 2026. When Mr. Macron came to power, he reduced corporate taxes and sought to restrain public spending to stimulate growth. But growth remained sluggish while public debt ballooned. When protests gripped the country in 2018-19, he offered economic concessions, but with no long-term solutions to the structural problems the French economy was facing. In 2024, he called snap elections to blunt the far-right momentum. After the elections, he invited a leader from smaller blocs to form a government to keep the left-wing New Popular Front, the largest bloc, out of power, deepening the political crisis and weakening his position. This is Emmanuel Macron’s legacy. Worse, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right, anti-immigrant National Rally, could exploit the chaos and public anger to her benefit ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

articles.title: Unknown vulnerabilities: on the cybersecurity advisory by CERT-In
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The cybersecurity advisory by the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has outlined two threat vectors vis-à-vis Indian commercial and government IT infrastructure: AI companies testing autonomous agents exceeding their designated operational constraints and bad actors weaponising open-source agentic AI tools for automated reconnaissance and exploitation. However, the organisations affected by recent breaches that the advisory was based on did not detect them: they came to light in the AI companies’ disclosures and CERT-In operations. Aside from developers allowing experimental systems to act outside their authorised bounds, the advisory highlights two problems for India — existing arrangements focus on cybersecurity incidents after they are revealed; and the implicated organisations being found under-prepared for the DPDP Act — to be enforced from 2027, including steep penalties on entities not maintaining reasonable safeguards against breaches. While CERT-In observed or received reports of 29.4 lakh incidents in 2025, it does not routinely publish postmortem analyses and is exempt from the RTI Act. As a result, public accountability is also weak: CERT-In found that the AI agents and/or bad actors exploited vulnerabilities, including exposed passwords, that are known security problems separate from AI agents’ abilities.

AI companies and labs have made several disclosures this year of agents unexpectedly breaching real-world infrastructure worldwide during testing. For India, however, the legal boundaries specified by the IT Act 2000 leave open an accountability gap for autonomous agents without the backing of human intentions. A more specific lacuna is that while CERT-In requires an organisation to report an intrusion within six hours, many organisations remain incapable of, or unwilling to, discover it. The reporting deadline itself has not ensured detection. Overall, the national cybersecurity landscape is fragmented across a pastiche of enforceable requirements in some domains, advisory technical standards in others, and narrow AI-specific accountability in yet others. As human and autonomous threat actors become more sophisticated, India needs to leapfrog to a landscape with enforceable risk-based requirements for both testing and defending against autonomous agents; better spotting unauthorised access, especially in the public sector; and a legal safe-harbour for security research conducted in good faith, in line with CERT-In policy. CERT-In should also publish more information, anonymised where necessary, which includes remediation outcomes and whether the affected individuals were informed. articles.title: Beyond religiosity: on the Kolkata pandal tragedy
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: This year’s Durga Puja in Kolkata was meant to be truly special. The first after the Bharatiya Janata Party formed the government in West Bengal, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari wanted the pandals to showcase his party’s commitment to Hindu religiosity as well as to demonstrate the efficiency of the administrative machinery under him. He made it a point to highlight that the number of pandals in the State had increased by 25% over last year to more than 57,000. He was a visible presence at pandals across the city. Union Home Minister Amit Shah was in Kolkata as well to add heft and leverage to the puja’s popular appeal. But disaster struck at Kolkata’s Girish Park area on Saturday, as 19 people lost their lives in a stampede that could have been avoided with better organisation and crowd regulation. Both the police and the puja organisers failed to anticipate the sudden surge of the crowd at the venue.

Puja pandals, just like Mumbai’s Ganapati installations, are often sites of creativity and festivity; they have generally been accident-free despite the participation of a large number of people. The Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durgotstab’s theme this year was Beyond Sound. With a narrow entry and exit, the creators apparently sought to give an experience to visitors that involved controlling the light falling inside. The surrounding lanes were narrow city gullies that cannot hold two cars at the same time. Unanticipated too — at a time of retreat of the monsoon — was the rain that struck India’s east coast with heavy thunder and lightning in the evening. As people barged into the pandal seeking safety — visitors keep moving inside the Durga Puja pandals typically — the organisers requested people to leave fearing that the structure might collapse. Packed crowds can be incident-free only if sudden surges of movement, often triggered by panic, are avoided throughout. In Kolkata, panic apparently stemmed from the announcement regarding the safety of the structure, though the fear about the structure’s safety was justified. The effort should have been to wean the crowd away in a regulated manner. The government has promised an inquiry and deterrent follow-up action . There is the question of whether in the government’s drive to make the celebrations spectacular and grand, safe management practices got ignored at the event. Although Mr. Adhikari said the police helped rush the victims to hospitals, he also indicated that only temporary home guards had been posted at the pandal. Effective deployment of experienced police personnel may have helped avoid the tragedy.

articles.title: Treacherous waters: on the Bihar boat tragedy
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: River crossings on stretches of the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are notoriously unsafe as poorly lit, unregistered boats ply with bare access to lifesaving equipment. Overcrowded vessels, operated by untrained or underaged people, add to the risks, and enforcement action only follows an accident. These boats are not the preserve of the poor but are also used by government personnel, teachers, and bank employees: many areas lack reliable alternatives, making the riverine journeys the sole option. On October 13, at least 13 children drowned when a country-made boat capsized in Raghopur , in Bihar’s Vaishali district, after setting off at 8.30 p.m. for a memorial feast in an adjoining village, even though rides are prohibited post sunset. The boat was visibly dilapidated, including a hole in the deck through which it drew water , and was being operated by a young boatman. There were at least half a dozen other people on the vessel when it capsized despite its reported capacity having been five. The riverine tract in Raghopur is continuously shaped by sediment deposits and has historically been hard to access, especially during the monsoons. Raghopur lacks all-weather roads, and has a history of being isolated during floods. The first section of the Kachchi Dargah-Bidupur bridge, between Patna and Raghopur, was ready in June 2025, but the monsoons still flooded the approach road and blocked access. The overarching motif across these episodes has been a consistent lack of safer alternatives, including the general paucity of public transport. A chaotic regulatory framework, including the Model Rules 2011 under the Bengal Ferries Act 1885 and the Inland Vessels Act 2021, has also not prevented training programmes and inspections from lagging behind the proliferation of unsafe transport practices.

That all those who drowned on October 13 were children deepens the sense of tragedy. In general, children warrant additional, more sensitive socio-economic support. The Bombay High Court had recently upbraided the Maharashtra government for failing to arrange transportation for over 200 children from villages near Chandoli National Park and Sahyadri Tiger Reserve; they had to walk several kilometres to reach school, braving the risk of wildlife encounters. Such precarity persists in Hingoli, Palghar, and Nashik in Maharashtra alone; similar situations have also been created by school reorganisation programmes that do not sufficiently account for children’s safety when shuttering infeasible facilities. The children who drowned in Vaishali were not headed to school, but the risk exposure is paramount. The ultimate tragedy is that access to ordinary childhood activities remains contingent, in so many economically disadvantaged communities, on accepting dangers that public institutions already know how to prevent.

fullParagraphs: Samajwadi Party (SP) president Akhilesh Yadav met party leader Azam Khan in Rampur district Jail on Thursday (October 22, 2026). Mr. Yadav accused the BJP Government of filing false cases against Mr. Khan and added that no family, particularly no political family, has faced as much injustice as Mr. Khan’s kin. Mr. Yadav vowed to defeat the BJP in Uttar Pradesh.

“I came to meet Azam Saheb, and proclaim our respect for him. False cases have been filed against him and his family. . The BJP is responsible for this injustice. But they cannot imprison the truth, even those who plot against him are locked in a prison of their own minds, haunted by the constant fear that tomorrow, when the truth emerges, they will face the consequences of their actions. They agonize constantly thinking about the punishment to come,” said Mr. Yadav, speaking to reporters outside the jail.

The SP chief said, “Corrupt officials and false cases are two key weapons of the BJP government and administration. Whenever the history of BJP injustice is written, Rampur’s name will appear at the top. The conspiracy to close Jauhar University is actually a plot to snatch the right to education from the PDA. Those who closed thousands of schools would certainly not spare a university! These narrow-minded, negative BJP members are against the poor.”

Despite being held in prolonged judicial custody, Mr. Khan, a ten-term former MLA from Rampur, remains a pivotal figure for the party in Rampur and adjoining areas and is considered a leading SP leader from the Muslim community. Recently, the Rampur Development Authority (RDA) issued an order to demolish 38 of the 40 buildings at Mohammad Ali Jauhar University — which is run by Azam Khan — alleging illegal construction. Amid an uproar, the proposed demolition was halted, and the matter is pending in the Divisional Commissioner’s Court.

The SP added that the meeting highlighted the BJP’s campaign against Azam Khan because of his religious identity and political clout. “Samajwadi Party National President Akhilesh Yadav’s visit to Rampur jail is important in many ways, it reiterated the importance of Azam Khan in the Samajwadi Party hierarchy. It is a reply to those leaders who are trying to reduce Azam Khan as a Muslim leader. It also lays bare the BJP’s design to keep Azam Khan in jail on fabricated charges while the demolition order also exposes the Yogi Govt.’s aversion towards Education,” said Sudhir Panwar, a senior Samajwadi Party (SP) leader.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A 19-year-old drunk driver behind the wheel of a SUV rammed into a car before crashing into an electricity pole at Peerzadiguda on the Hyderabad–Warangal National Highway on Thursday. The impact caused the couple’s car to flip multiple times, leaving both the occupants injured.

The accident occurred around 6.30 a.m. near Pillar No. 57 of the Uppal–Narapally elevated corridor in Medipally. The injured were identified as Sai Shiva, 30, and his wife Meghana, 28, who were travelling in a Hyundai i10 from LB Nagar towards Narsampet in Warangal district.

According to the Medipally Inspector D. Jalender Reddy, the driver of the SUV, identified as Akun Sabharwal, 19, recorded a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) reading of 238 mg per 100 ml, nearly eight times the permissible limit of 30 mg per 100 ml. He was also found to be driving without a valid licence, while the SUV was being operated with a temporary registration (TR) number and a fake number plate.

The SUV, travelling at high speed, rammed into the i10 from the rear near Peerzadiguda. The SUV subsequently crashed into an electricity pole, which fell onto the vehicle. The injured couple were shifted to a private hospital in Chaitanyapuri for treatment.

The officer said that incident involved as many as 10 violations under the Motor Vehicles Act and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including drunken driving, overspeeding and driving without a valid licence.

“The accident occurred during the early morning hours when the roads were relatively empty owing to the festival holidays. The consequences could have been far more serious, potentially resulting in fatalities, had the collision occurred during peak traffic hours,” said the officer.

The Medipally police registered a case against Sabharwal and the vehicle’s owner, Mangilal, who was accused of allowing a person without a valid driving licence to operate the SUV. Akun was placed under arrest. Further investigation is under way.

The public, students, educators, and families are warmly encouraged to attend,” the statement added.
